1219.title: Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308)
1219.hook: every creature has its own thisness, loved by God
1219.howItsDone: Franciscans study Duns Scotus as one of their order's great teachers, and the Church has beatified him as Blessed John Duns Scotus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonaventure's mind: think as far as you can, then let love take the last step. Your line was love goes further.

Two sparrows land on a fence. Same kind, same size, same brown feathers, same tilt of the head. A bird book would describe them in exactly the same words. And yet one is this sparrow, and the other is that one. If one flies away, the one left behind isn't a copy. It's itself. What makes it that? That small question, the kind a child might ask, occupied the teachers of the Middle Ages, and one Franciscan friar gave it an answer that came to be known by a strange, lovely word.
screen: `TWO SPARROWS ON A FENCE.` → `THIS ONE, AND THAT ONE.` → `WHAT MAKES IT ITSELF?`

segments.voice: The friar is John Duns Scotus, a teacher at Oxford and Paris, remembered as the Subtle Doctor. For him and for Thomas Aquinas alike, the two sparrows share one nature: they're both sparrows. The question was what makes each one an individual. Aquinas, the Dominican teacher, pointed to matter: this sparrow is made of this bit of the world, and that one of that bit. Scotus thought there had to be something more. Something positive in each creature that belongs to it alone, not a leftover, not a label, but the real heart of its being this one. The Latin word tied to his teaching is haecceitas. In English, haecceity: thisness. Why would a friar care? Because of Francis, who didn't love birds in general. He talked to these birds, on this road, and called one particular wolf his brother. Scotus gives that habit a philosophy. If each creature has its own thisness, then God doesn't make and love things in bulk, as samples of a kind. God knows and wills each one as itself. Jesus says something close in the gospel: not one sparrow is forgotten before God, and even the hairs of your head are numbered. And the prophet Isaiah hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims, "called thee by thy name: thou art mine." Much later the poet Gerard Manley Hopkins, a Jesuit priest, took Scotus to heart and wrote poems about each thing crying out its own self. Readers still weigh Scotus's answer against Aquinas's. But on Scotus's account, nobody is a duplicate. Not the sparrow, not you.
screen: `SAME KIND, DIFFERENT ONE.` · `AQUINAS: MATTER. SCOTUS: SOMETHING MORE.` · `HAECCEITY: THISNESS.` · `GOD LOVES EACH ONE AS ITSELF.` · then, large: `CALLED THEE BY THY NAME: THOU ART MINE.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing near you, a mug, a leaf, your own hand, and instead of the category it belongs to, look at this one: the chip on the rim, the particular vein, the scar on the knuckle. Keep looking until it stops being a mug and becomes this mug, the only one with exactly this history. If you pray, thank God for making it, and you, one at a time; if you don't, simply let it be itself.

1220.title: Christ, first in God's plan
1220.hook: Franciscan thinkers held Christ would have come even without sin; others disagree
1220.howItsDone: Catholics are free to hold either view on why the Son of God became man; theologians in the line of Scotus teach the primacy of Christ, and theologians in the line of Aquinas teach that the Incarnation was willed as the remedy for sin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Duns Scotus and his strange word, haecceity: thisness. Your line was this one.

Here's a question with no way to check the answer. Suppose Adam and Eve had never sinned. Would there still have been a Christmas? It sounds like a question for a sleepless night, but medieval teachers took it seriously, because the answer says something about why Christ came at all. Was he God's rescue plan, sent because things went wrong? Or was he the plan from the beginning? Today, two honest answers.
screen: `WHAT IF NO ONE HAD SINNED?` → `WOULD THERE STILL BE CHRISTMAS?` → `RESCUE, OR THE PLAN?`

segments.voice: Start with Thomas Aquinas. He notices that whenever Scripture gives a reason for the Son of God becoming man, the reason is sin: he came to save. So, Aquinas says, it's more fitting to say that if humanity had not sinned, the Incarnation would not have happened. And he adds a careful line: God's power isn't limited by that. God could have done it anyway. The Church sings something close to this view at the Easter Vigil, in a hymn that calls Adam's sin a happy fault, because it won so great a Redeemer. Now Duns Scotus, the Franciscan, from yesterday. He comes at it from love, not from the problem. God, he says, does things in order. When you plan a house, you think of the house first and the bricks after. God's first and highest intention, the thing all of creation is for, is Christ: the Son joined to a human nature, the masterpiece of God's love. Everything else is willed for his sake. So Christ wasn't a patch for a broken plan. He was the plan. Sin changed the way he came, as a Redeemer who suffered. But he would have come. Scotus leans on Paul's letter to the Colossians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature: For in him were all things created." Franciscan thinkers after Scotus took this up as their own. Both answers are held by Catholics, and the Church hasn't chosen between them. One sees Christ as the rescuer who came because we fell. The other sees him as the reason there was a world to fall in.
screen: `AQUINAS: HE CAME BECAUSE OF SIN.` · `O HAPPY FAULT.` · `SCOTUS: CHRIST WAS WILLED FIRST.` · `BOTH ANSWERS HELD; NONE CHOSEN.` · then, large: `THE FIRSTBORN OF EVERY CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Hold the two pictures side by side: in one, the world goes wrong and Christ comes to set it right; in the other, the world was made with Christ in mind from the start. Notice which one your mind leans toward, then let both rest. If you pray, simply thank God for Christ, however the plan was drawn; if you don't, stay with the question and the breath.

1221.title: The Franciscan crown
1221.hook: a seven-decade rosary of Mary's joys
1221.howItsDone: Franciscans and other Catholics pray the Franciscan crown on a seven-decade rosary, meditating on the seven joys of Mary, one joy for each decade.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Christ in God's plan: a rescue after the fall, or the plan from the start? Your line was christ first.

A young man has a habit. Every so often he picks wildflowers, weaves them into a little crown, and sets it on the head of a statue of Mary. Then he joins the Franciscans, and in the friary there's no time for flower-picking. The crowns stop. He's heartbroken, so much so, the story goes, that he thinks about leaving. Then, as he prays, Mary appears to him. Don't be sad, she tells him. Instead of flowers that wither, weave me a crown that won't: say your prayers in honor of seven joys of my life. That, tradition says, is how a new kind of rosary began.
screen: `A CROWN OF WILDFLOWERS.` → `NO MORE FLOWERS IN THE FRIARY.` → `A CROWN THAT WON'T WITHER.`

segments.voice: This path met the rosary's beads and decades long ago. The Franciscan crown, sometimes called the Seraphic rosary, has seven decades instead of five. Each decade is an Our Father and ten Hail Marys, and each holds a joy. The first is the Annunciation, when the angel Gabriel greets Mary, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." The second is the Visitation, Mary hurrying to her cousin Elizabeth and the child leaping in Elizabeth's womb. The third, the birth of Jesus. The fourth, the wise men coming to adore him. The fifth, finding the boy Jesus in the Temple after three days of searching. Those five come straight from Luke and Matthew. The last two come from the Church's tradition. The sixth is the risen Jesus appearing to his mother, a meeting the Gospels don't describe but tradition holds. The seventh is Mary's Assumption into heaven and her crowning as queen. The usual rosary's mysteries take in sorrows as well as joys and glories. This one stays with joy. It isn't that Franciscans deny sorrow; tradition says Francis bore the wounds of Christ in his own body. But the family that told of perfect joy at a locked gate also made a rosary of pure gladness, and gave it to Mary as a crown. And joy, here, isn't a mood. It's a list of things that happened: a greeting, a visit, a birth, a homecoming, a reunion. Each bead is a reason.
screen: `SEVEN DECADES, SEVEN JOYS.` · `FIVE FROM THE GOSPELS.` · `TWO FROM THE CHURCH'S TRADITION.` · `A ROSARY THAT STAYS WITH JOY.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.`

segments.voice: If you pray the rosary, say seven Hail Marys, one for each of Mary's joys: the greeting, the visit, the birth, the wise men, the boy found, the risen son, the crown. If you don't, count seven joys from your own life on your fingers: a phone call that came, a child born, a reunion. Go slowly, and let each one be a bead.
The Franciscan crown. A seven-decade rosary, a garland of Hail Marys woven around seven joys of Mary. Today's word.
Your line: seven joys. A crown of prayers that won't wither, the story says. Until tomorrow.

1222.title: Keepers of the Holy Land
1222.hook: brown-robed friars who keep watch over the places of Jesus's life, and the walk they brought home
1222.howItsDone: Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross in parish churches, especially on the Fridays of Lent, walking or turning from one station to the next; in Jerusalem, Franciscan friars lead the walk through the streets of the old city.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Franciscan crown, a rosary that walks through Mary's joys. Your line was seven joys.

A brown habit. A rope belt with knots in it. Sandals. That outfit belongs to Assisi, to Francis and his brothers. But you can also meet it in the stone streets of Jerusalem, Bethlehem and Nazareth, on a friar who isn't visiting. He lives there. He sweeps a shrine, unlocks a door for pilgrims at dawn, and sings the hours in a chapel built over a place from the Gospels. Tradition says the brothers of Francis have kept watch over these places for centuries. Today, those keepers, and the walk they carried home.
screen: `A BROWN HABIT, A ROPE BELT.` → `IN JERUSALEM, NOT ASSISI.` → `HE ISN'T VISITING. HE LIVES THERE.`

segments.voice: Back on day one hundred fifty, you met the Stations; today, the friars behind them. They call their charge the Custody of the Holy Land, and the brother who leads them is the Custos, the keeper. The job is plain and endless: care for the shrines, pray in them, and welcome pilgrims with sore feet. Some of the holiest places aren't theirs alone. The church over Calvary and the empty tomb is shared by several Christian churches, Orthodox and Armenian and others alongside the Catholics, each with its own corners and hours. So keeping the Holy Land means keeping the peace in it. Then there's the walk. In Jerusalem, pilgrims wanted to follow the road Jesus took to the cross, stopping to pray. Luke tells one of those stops. Women follow him, weeping, and he turns to them. In the Douay-Rheims: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." But not everyone can get to that street. So the walk was carried home. The friars helped spread the Stations of the Cross, crosses or pictures on a church wall, so a grandmother in a village could walk the road to Calvary in her own parish. A surprise on that wall: some stops come straight from the Gospels, like Simon of Cyrene taking up the cross, and some from tradition, like Veronica wiping his face. The Gospels never mention her. The Stations hold both, and the friars kept both.

segments.voice: Stand if you can, take a few slow steps and stop, and bring to mind Jesus handed over to die; a few more steps, and Simon, a stranger pulled from the crowd to carry the cross; a few more, and the women on the road, and the words he said to them. If you pray, say an Our Father at the last stop; if not, just stand still and let the road be quiet.

1223.title: The Capuchins (1528)
1223.hook: a reform with hoods, beards and poverty; Padre Pio was one
1223.howItsDone: Capuchin friars live in community under the Rule of Saint Francis, and are often found in parishes, soup kitchens, hospitals and confessionals; Catholics who are devoted to Saint Pio of Pietrelcina often ask his prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keepers of the Holy Land, and the walk they carried home. Your line was the custody.

In old paintings of the saints, some friars look wilder than the rest: a full beard, a long pointed hood, bare feet in sandals, a rough habit patched where it wore through. That's on purpose. Inside the family of Francis, a group of brothers came to believe the order had drifted from the poverty he loved. They wanted to go back: to hermitages and begging, to preaching in plain words to plain people. They took up a hood shaped the way they believed Francis wore his, and people gave them a nickname for it. Today's word is that nickname.
screen: `A BEARD, A HOOD, BARE FEET.` → `THE ORDER HAD DRIFTED.` → `GO BACK TO FRANCIS.`

segments.voice: Capuchin. Tradition says the name comes from the Italian word for that hood. The street chose it, and it stuck. What they wanted was simple and hard: to live the Rule of Francis without the comforts that had crept in. Smaller houses, fewer things, long hours of silent prayer, then out among ordinary people. The early years weren't easy. The reform had opponents inside the Franciscan family, and for a time it wasn't clear it would survive. It did, and it stayed in the family: Capuchins are Franciscans, one branch of the same tree, following the same Rule. Tradition remembers them staying when sickness came to a town, nursing the dying when others fled. You met one Capuchin back on day nine hundred five: Padre Pio, in southern Italy, whom the Church honors as Saint Pio of Pietrelcina. People traveled from far away to stand in long lines for his confessional. There were reports that he bore wounds like Christ's, and the Church looked into them with care and caution. But what drew people was often simpler: a poor friar in a brown hood who would listen to the worst thing you had done. It echoes Jesus in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come to me, all you that labour, and are burdened, and I will refresh you." The reform kept pointing at the same thing: go back to the poor man of Assisi, and then go out.
screen: `A NICKNAME FROM THE STREET.` · `LIVE THE RULE WITHOUT THE COMFORTS.` · `STILL FRANCISCANS: ONE BRANCH, ONE TREE.` · `PADRE PIO AND THE LONG LINES.` · then, large: `AND I WILL REFRESH YOU.`

segments.voice: Picture one Capuchin somewhere today, in a soup line, a hospital corridor, a confessional with the little light on, waiting for whoever comes. Then bring to mind someone in your own life who listens to other people's burdens, a nurse, a counselor, a priest, a friend everyone calls. If you pray, pray for the Capuchins and for that person, in your own words or with an Our Father; if not, just hold them both kindly.

1224.title: Patron of ecology (1979)
1224.hook: John Paul II names Francis patron of those who care for creation
1224.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Francis in early October, and some parishes bless animals on or near that day; Catholic groups who work for the care of creation often take Francis as their patron.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Capuchins, a hooded reform that went back to Francis's poverty. Your line was the hooded friars.

Brother Sun. Sister Moon and the stars. Brother Wind. Sister Water. Brother Fire. It sounds like a roll call at a family reunion, and in a way it is. These are the names Francis gives the world in a song in his own Italian dialect, the Canticle of the Creatures. Tradition says he made it near the end of his life, sick, his eyes so bad he could barely stand the light. A man who could hardly see the sun called it his brother. Centuries later, a pope looked at that song and gave Francis a new job. Today's word is the job.

segments.voice: Pope John Paul II named Francis the patron of those who care for creation, the patron of ecology. A patron, for Catholics, is a saint in heaven asked to pray for a particular people or work. So anyone who plants a tree has, in Catholic eyes, a friend in brown. Why Francis? Because of the Canticle. It praises God for the sun, beautiful and radiant, who brings the day. For wind and air and every kind of weather. For water, useful and humble and precious and pure. For fire, bright and strong, who lights the night. Then comes the surprise. Francis doesn't call the earth brother. He calls her our sister and our mother, who feeds us and brings forth fruit and colored flowers and grass. Our line borrows the family word; the point is kinship. For Francis, creation isn't scenery. It's family, all of it singing back to its maker. The Bible gives the job from the start. In Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, God puts the man in the garden "to dress it, and to keep it." To tend it and guard it, not to own it. And the book of Daniel has a song inviting every creature in: "All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord." So a patron of ecology isn't a saint of recycling bins. He's a saint who heard the world praying, and took his place in the choir.

1225.title: The peace prayer, honestly
1225.hook: the prayer that asks to be made an instrument of peace wasn't written by Francis, though it's Franciscan in spirit
1225.howItsDone: Catholics and other Christians pray the peace prayer at home, in schools, and at weddings, funerals and public gatherings; Franciscans greet one another with words of peace drawn from Francis's Testament.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the patron of ecology, and a song that calls the sun brother. Your line was brother earth.

It's on the fridge magnet. It's on the framed print in the parish hall, under a friar with a bird on his hand. It's read at weddings and funerals and sung at school Masses. It begins by asking God to make the one who prays an instrument of peace, and it often carries a name at the bottom: Saint Francis. Here's the honest part, and it's the whole lesson. Francis didn't write it. So why does it carry his name, and does that change what it's worth?
screen: `ON THE FRIDGE, AT THE WEDDING.` → `SIGNED: SAINT FRANCIS.` → `HE DIDN'T WRITE IT.`

segments.voice: Way back on day seventeen, you met the prayer that bears his name; today, its real story. First, the prayer. It asks to be made an instrument of peace. Then it walks through pairs: where there is hatred, let me bring love; injury, pardon; doubt, faith; despair, hope; darkness, light; sadness, joy. Then it turns around, asking to seek less to be comforted than to comfort, to be understood than to understand, to be loved than to love. It ends with reversals: in giving we receive, in pardoning we are pardoned, in dying we are born to eternal life. Now the history, as historians trace it. The prayer turns up long after Francis, in French, in a small church magazine, with no author's name. Later it was printed on a card with a picture of Francis, and the name traveled with the picture. No one seems to have meant to deceive; a prayer just found a face. A fake? Not quite. It isn't by Francis, but it's shaped like him. In his Testament, Francis says God showed him a greeting: the Lord give you peace. He walked into a war camp to meet a sultan. And the prayer's reversals sound like the man who said bitter became sweet. Jesus says it in the Beatitudes, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." So pray it with both hands open: not his words, but his shape.
screen: `AN INSTRUMENT OF PEACE, IN PAIRS.` · `FIRST FOUND IN FRENCH, UNSIGNED.` · `A PRAYER THAT FOUND A FACE.` · `NOT HIS WORDS, BUT HIS SHAPE.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.`

segments.voice: If you know the peace prayer, pray it slowly, knowing it comes from an unnamed hand and not from Assisi. If you don't, take one pair: bring to mind one place in your life where there is hatred, injury or sadness, hold it for a few breaths, and set beside it the word the prayer pairs with it, love, pardon or joy; if you pray, offer that pair to God, and if not, let the two words sit side by side.
The peace prayer. A prayer to be made an instrument of peace, not written by Francis, but carrying his shape and his greeting. Today's word.
